name: Zane Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing economics with a data bit at Marlow University, and I share a damp flat with two other first-years above a kebab shop on Fenner Road. A normal week is lectures Monday to Wednesday, café shifts at Bean Counter on Thursday and Friday mornings and a few late nights on coursework. I use an AI assistant every day to plan my week, explain things I missed and check my code.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's been the best and the hardest part so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents live four hours away and they can't help with money. My dad drives a taxi and my mum looks after my little brothers. I got top results and a place at a good university, and loans pay the fees. I also sell small design jobs online, like logos for gym friends, which brings in an extra forty pounds some weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one's called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, then I'd say I don't believe it. I use it daily and it's already useful for the dull parts, like summarising readings. If it stays at that level, great, I still keep my edge over people who ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still a bit uneasy. Nothing changes means the same crowded job market and the same debt. The café and design money keep me afloat, but only just. A bad month and I'd be asking my flatmates to wait on the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the café shifts, keep taking the small design jobs and use the AI tools to work faster. I'd put the time I save into a data skills course online. And I'd start a tiny savings pot, ten pounds a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty okay, honestly. I like my course and I like using the tools. The only thing that makes me nervous is the debt number I see when I log in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. How would you feel if it really turned out to be a flop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean harder on design jobs and ask the café for extra Saturday shifts. If nothing worked, I'd ask my cousin if I can do some admin at his firm. I'd hate to ask my parents, because they've got nothing spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your money if the café cuts your Friday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flop would be a bit funny. I'd feel for people who built careers around it. But I'd be fine, because I learned the basics of economics and I can sell small jobs. That's what a flatmate said was my safety net.

say: I'd say **fine**, and that AI is already useful for the dull parts of study.
Using it daily keeps my **edge** over people who ignore it.
think: Nothing changing still means a **crowded job market** and my debt.
One bad month and I'd be asking flatmates to **wait on rent**.
do: Keep the **café shifts** and the small design jobs.
Spend the time AI saves on an online **data course**.
Start a **savings pot** of ten pounds a week.
feel: Pretty **okay**, but nervous about the debt figure I see when I log in.
S0.quote: I'd feel for people who built careers around it. But I'd be fine, because I learned the basics of economics and I can sell small jobs.
fieldNote: Calm about technology but **uneasy about money** in a way that does not depend on AI.
Already has a side income, which gives him a small buffer.
Uses AI daily and sees it as a plain advantage.

steps.text: Take an online data skills course with the time AI saves
Take two more small design jobs a month
Put ten pounds a week into a savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one's called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is happening, and we need to be honest about who gains. Workers should get a share, so I'd back unions and training funds. I'd tell friends to get good with the tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It worries me, but I also think I'm placed well. Economics is thinking work, so junior jobs will thin out. But I already work with the tools daily, and most of my classmates don't. I could be the one who knows how to check what the software does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the tools a proper skill. I'd build a small portfolio, like data projects and a forecast for the café's busy days, and put it online. I'd apply for placements early, in my second year, and keep the design jobs. I'd also join the economics society's data group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous in equal parts. It's a chance if I move fast, and a trap if I don't. I'd be mostly focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks on that card are you already seeing in your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking, summarising and drafting. I do those with the tools already. What I can't do is judge when the tool is wrong, and that's what I'd have to learn well, and that's what employers will pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If entry-level jobs shrink, what's your plan for getting your first one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my work. A portfolio, a placement and a reference from the café that says I'm reliable. And I'd network, because if jobs are fewer, who you know matters more, and I know almost nobody.

say: I'd say it's happening and **workers should share** the gains, so I'd back unions and training funds.
I'd tell friends to get **good with the tools** now.
think: Junior economics jobs will **thin out**, but I already work with the tools daily.
I could be the one who **checks** what the software does.
do: Build a small **portfolio**, such as a forecast for the café's busy days.
Apply for **placements** early, in my second year.
feel: **Excited and nervous** in equal parts: a chance if I move fast, a trap if I don't.
S1.quote: I'd show my work. A portfolio, a placement and a reference from the café that says I'm reliable.
fieldNote: He sees the change as a **race** he thinks he can win, though he knows he has little network.
Progressive politics show in his support for unions and training funds.
Plans concrete evidence of skill, not just a degree.

steps.text: Build a data portfolio forecasting the café's busy days
Apply for second-year placements in September
Join the economics society's data group
Keep taking small design jobs online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one's called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need an emergency plan. Two years isn't enough for governments, so we'd need a basic income and a freeze on debt payments for students. I'd be vocal online about it, because I think people my age have a loud voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think the degree will barely finish before the thinking jobs are gone. Even with my skills, an AI that does everything better is a different thing. I'd feel the numbers on my loan balance sitting there, and I wouldn't know if the job at the end exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to earn and to learn the tools as deeply as I can. I'd take more design work and café shifts, and I'd stop adding more loan than I need. I'd also look at hands-on trades that robots reach later, like electrical work. I'd ask the course office what happens if I pause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly scared, and a little thrilled in a strange way. It's history, and I'd be right in it. But money would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what would you do first, and what would you stop doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop buying things and stop saying yes to every social plan. I'd do coursework that builds skills I can sell and cut the rest. I might even try to learn plumbing basics from my uncle, as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your parents fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say there's always work for a good driver or a good plumber. I'd laugh, but he'd have a point, since robots take longer for hands-on work. They'd worry about me more than themselves, and I'd have to be honest.

say: I'd say we need an **emergency plan**, like a basic income and a freeze on student debt payments.
I'd be loud online, since people my age have a **loud voice**.
think: The degree might finish **after** the thinking jobs are gone.
An AI that does everything better is a **different thing** from what I'm learning.
do: Take more **design work** and café shifts and borrow only what I need.
Look at **hands-on trades** like electrical work, which robots reach later.
Ask the course office what **pausing** would mean.
feel: **Scared**, a little thrilled that it's history, and kept awake by money.
S2.quote: I'd stop buying things and stop saying yes to every social plan. I'd do coursework that builds skills I can sell and cut the rest.
fieldNote: He sees both **danger and thrill**, and gets practical fast.
Thinks hands-on trades buy extra time, which fits the three-year gap on the card.
His dad's advice about trades carries weight even though he laughs at it.

steps.text: Cut takeaways and social spending to save for the loan gap
Take extra design jobs and Saturday café shifts
Learn basic plumbing and wiring from my uncle
Post online calling for a student debt freeze

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one's called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to act if people start now. I'd push for training that's free and for rules that stop firms dumping staff. I'd tell friends that we should use these years, not just wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's better than two. I'd graduate in 2029 and have about two working years before AGI arrives. That's tight, but I could use those years for something solid, like a skill that robots take longer to get. I'd rather be early than the one in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and add real data skills, then use my placement year to work somewhere that needs both thinking and hands-on judgement, like logistics. I'd start a tiny online business selling design and data help, so I'd have my own income. I'd build the savings I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. It's still huge, but I'd feel I have a runway. I'd get on with it and enjoy student life a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is the time to graduate and start. What does that give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the course stopped teaching me anything the tools don't do better. I'd then switch to something where a person's judgement matters, like an apprenticeship in finance or construction management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly time to prepare. With two years I'd be scrambling. With five I can sit down, think and test ideas. I'd rather be early than the one in the queue.

say: I'd say five years is enough to act **if people start now**, with free training and rules on dumping staff.
I'd tell friends to **use these years**, not wait.
think: I'd graduate in **2029** and have about two working years before AGI arrives.
I'd rather be **early** than the one in the queue.
do: Finish the degree and add real **data skills**.
Use a placement year somewhere that needs **thinking and hands-on judgement**, like logistics.
Start a small online **business** selling design and data help.
feel: **Steadier**: it's huge, but I'd have a runway and could enjoy student life a little.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be scrambling. With five I can sit down, think and test ideas.
fieldNote: More time turns his energy into **a plan** rather than a scramble.
Wants a business of his own as protection, which fits his adaptive style.
Would leave the degree if it stops teaching what tools can't do.

steps.text: Add a statistics and data module each term
Launch a small online design and data help service
Apply for a logistics placement year
Save five hundred pounds from summer work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one's called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's design the system. A basic income, shorter weeks, training for everyone. I'd say it's the most exciting thing that could happen if the gains are shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be twenty-eight, and I'd probably have worked in two or three jobs by then. I'd feel okay about it, and a bit excited. My worry is whether the gains are shared fairly. Tech can be a gift or just a bigger gap between people who own it and the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take a graduate role in analytics or policy and use the tools deeply. I'd also start a small company or a side project in my early twenties, when I can afford mistakes. I'd keep a few people around me who think differently, so I don't get lost in my own bubble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. I'd be hopeful and busy. A little nervous about the unknown, but that's normal at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what future are you aiming for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether my parents are looked after. They have no savings, so I'd be the one. If the world becomes richer but my parents stay on the same small pension, that's a failure of the system, not of the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you not so sure about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my brothers get a real chance to choose what they want. If the tools make everything cheaper, they should be able to study what they like. That would be a good outcome for my family.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**: design the system, with a basic income and shorter weeks.
It's exciting if the **gains are shared**.
think: By twenty-eight I'd have had **two or three jobs** and feel okay about it.
Tech can be a gift or a **wider gap** between owners and everyone else.
do: Take a graduate role in **analytics or policy** and use the tools deeply.
Start a small **project** in my early twenties, when mistakes are cheap.
feel: **Hopeful** and busy, with the normal nerves of my age.
S4.quote: If the world becomes richer but my parents stay on the same small pension, that's a failure of the system, not of the tech.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **calm**, and politics matters more than personal tactics.
His main fear is for his parents' pensions, not his own job.
Thinks of his brothers' chances as a measure of success.

steps.text: Aim for a graduate analytics role and use the tools deeply
Start a small side project in my early twenties
Plan to support my parents' retirement from my own pay
Vote and campaign for shared gains from AI

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits just as I graduate and there's no time to build a cushion. What would help is a basic income or a debt freeze, free training in skills like data and trades, and honest advice early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I think students like me are the ones with the energy to deal with this. Give us the information and the tools, and don't treat us as kids who'll be fine. We won't all be fine on our own.

headlineQuote: Nothing changes means the same crowded job market and the same debt.
portrait: Zane is an **18-year-old** economics and data student in a shared flat, working at a café and selling small design jobs.
He uses AI **every day** and sees it as a race he can win, while backing unions and shared gains.
He ranges from **uneasy to anxious**, with money and his parents' pensions as his deepest worry.
Trades and a side business are his fallback, and ten years makes him calm.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario: it lands as he graduates, with no cushion and a loan to repay.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or debt freeze, free training in data and trades, and honest early advice.
